subject: Critical Thinking
title: Framing: How the Same Story Becomes Two Truths
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Framing: How the Same Story Becomes Two Truths.

hook.text: 'Unemployment falls to 5%' and '1 in 20 workers can't find a job.' Same fact. Completely different emotional impact.

buildup.text: Framing: selecting which aspects of reality to emphasize, which to minimize, and which to omit entirely.

discovery.text: George Lakoff: political frames are so powerful that facts presented outside the frame are literally not processed.

twist.text: 'Tax relief' frames taxes as a burden. 'Revenue investment' frames them as a tool.

climax.text: When consuming media, ask: 'What frame is being used? What would this look like in a different frame?'

punchline.text: You can't escape frames. But you can switch between them.

quiz.question: Why is media framing so powerful?
options: It determines which aspects of reality are emphasized, minimized, or omitted

details.summary: Framing determines which aspects of a story are emphasized and which are minimized, causing the same facts to produce opposite impressions. A protest can be framed as 'citizens exercising freedom' or 'mob disrupting order' using identical footage.
details.whyItMatters: Recognizing framing is essential because it is invisible by design. The frame tells you what to think about an issue before you even begin to evaluate it.
takeaways: Frames select, emphasize, and exclude aspects of reality
Two completely different narratives can be built from identical facts
Detecting the frame is the first step to independent analysis

faq.question: How does framing differ from outright lying or misinformation?
faq.answer: Framing uses true facts arranged to produce a desired impression. Nothing stated is false, but the selection and emphasis create a misleading picture. It is far more common and harder to detect than outright lies because everything said is technically true.

faq.question: What strategies can help you detect framing in news coverage?
faq.answer: Ask what information is absent: what would change your impression if included? Read coverage from opposing sources to see how the same facts produce different narratives. Notice the metaphors and analogies used, as they anchor perception.
